extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in an introduction-to-proofs course (Stanford CS103); anyone learning to write mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: A short checklist for writing clear, correct undergraduate-level mathematical proofs, covering what to state, variable introduction, sentence-level economy, style, and common logical pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly articulate assumptions and "want-to-shows"
rubrics_metrics.description: Every proof should make explicit: what is being assumed at the start; what is being proved (the goal / want-to-show); the proof technique chosen (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction). At each major step, restate the current want-to-show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state initial assumptions and the goal. Name the proof technique you will use (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction). When a proof contains major steps or subgoals, restate the current want-to-show so the reader can follow progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make each sentence load-bearing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Every statement in a proof should do one of the following things: set up a goal, introduce a new variable, or combine preceding results into something new."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove sentences that do not advance the argument or are never referenced again. Each sentence should either set up a subgoal, introduce and define a variable, or perform a logical combination / deduction from earlier statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and properly introduce variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Every variable must be classified as universally instantiated, existentially instantiated, or an explicitly chosen value. Use phrasing like "Let n be an arbitrary even integer" (universally instantiated), "There exists k such that n = 2k" (existentially instantiated), or "Let n = 6" (explicitly chosen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing variables use words such as "let", "consider", or "choose" rather than ambiguous phrases like "for every". Clearly indicate the scope of each variable so readers know whether it is arbitrary, exists, or fixed to a particular value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make specific claims about specific variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements must reference the specific variables in scope; avoid floating abstract claims. Manipulate concrete expressions, not high-level summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of vague assertions, write statements that quantify or name the variables you're manipulating. Work with explicit expressions (e.g., "write n = 2k for some integer k") rather than relying on informal summaries that hide which variables are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't repeat definitions; use them
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply each definition; don't restate it unnecessarily. (Bad example: "An even number is one of the form 2k. Therefore, since n is even..." Good example: "Since n is even, write n = 2k for some integer k.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than paraphrasing a definition and stopping, immediately instantiate and use the definition in your argument. Avoid restating the definition as if it were the argument itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in complete sentences and paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose should be grammatical English even if symbols are replaced by words (the "mugga mugga" test). No symbols-as-verbs. Proofs are paragraphs, not bullet lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the proof reads as coherent prose: every displayed formula should be embedded in sentence-level explanation. Avoid choppy fragments, telegraphic notes, and using symbols where a verb or clause is required. Structure longer proofs in paragraphs rather than a sequence of unconnected bulleted lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid quantifiers and propositional connectives in the prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use symbols like ∀, ∃, ⇒, ∧, ∨, ¬ in the prose; write out the words instead ("for all", "there exists", "implies", "and", "or", "not").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain English phrases for logical operators to make the argument readable. Avoid embedding symbolic logical notation into sentence text; reserve symbols for formal displayed expressions when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the "contradiction sandwich"
rubrics_metrics.description: If the body of an alleged contradiction proof is in fact a direct proof, present it directly. Don't wrap a direct argument inside "Suppose for contradiction... [direct proof]... but this contradicts our assumption."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve the contradiction structure only for genuine indirect arguments. If your steps directly establish the goal, rewrite the proof as a direct proof rather than needlessly framing it as a contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistakes the checklist catches
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-exhaustive list of frequent errors: variables used before being introduced; reuse of a variable name with a different meaning; implicit quantifier scope; conflating A = B as both equation and definition without saying which; missing case analysis; skipping a "back-substitute" at the end of an induction; using "clearly" / "obviously" to skip a step that the grader will not believe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this list as a diagnostic after drafting: check that every variable has been introduced before use, that names aren't overloaded, that quantifier scopes are explicit, that equalities are clearly identified as definitions versus identities, that all cases are handled, that inductive proofs include the back-substitution or closing step, and that no steps are elided with words like "clearly" or "obviously."
